A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Embodied Crowd Counting, ECCD, and ZECC. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes a checklist and Appendices A–F, all inspected.

before.justification: v1 reports original ECCD experiments, including navigation comparisons, component ablations, and parameter studies in Section 4.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation experiments and adds multi-view comparisons, occlusion analysis, and two real-world NLBN evaluations in Section 5 and Appendices D–F.

M1.justification: The core ATE, NLBN, and FDC procedures remain intact. Appendix F adds a real-drone adaptation using VGGT to reconstruct relative geometry and poses, followed by GPS-based conversion of NLBN waypoints into absolute navigation commands. Appendix C mainly documents previously unspecified implementation details.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 60-environment ECCD benchmark. v2 Appendix F extends evaluation beyond simulation to two real outdoor crowd scenes with drone observations and reconstructed geometry, introducing materially different input conditions. These tests evaluate NLBN viewpoint adjustment, rather than the complete autonomous ZECC pipeline.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates FBE, CoW, and OpenFMNav with GL or Grounding DINO. v2 retains these comparators and adds an entire multi-view counting comparison using MVF and CountFormer at three camera-grid spacings in Table 3. The changed CoW citation does not establish a different comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces multi-view camera grids at 10, 20, and 30 m with camera-count evaluation, travel-distance-limited exploration, an occlusion test with a 0.5 m threshold, and a manually annotated real-drone evaluation protocol. Existing sensitivity sweeps also change: navigation angles span 10–80 degrees in v1 Figure 6 versus 10–40 degrees in v2 Figure 5(b).

E4.justification: v2 retains the original component ablations but adds controlled travel-budget comparisons, trajectory case studies, quantitative obstruction analysis, an MLLM planning failure case, and real-world comparisons with and without NLBN. These directly examine efficiency, occlusion reduction, and failure conditions. The sensitivity analyses are also revised.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty bars. v2 adds ± values to Tables 2–3 and error bars to Figure 4, but does not specify run counts, seeds, or whether the uncertainty represents standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals. Additional runs therefore cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Overall results are revised: ZECC changes from 18.91% MAPE and 3804.63 m in v1 Table 1 to 18.71 ± 1.41% and 3722.45 ± 73.78 m in v2 Table 2. New results include MVC comparisons, real-world NLBN counting, and obstruction ratios of 4.52% for ZECC, 42.81% for OpenFMNav, and 21.77% for MVC-30. Sensitivity curves and reported cluster-size travel costs also change.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds a mathematical obstruction criterion using nearest-navigation-point vectors, projections, and a distance threshold in Equations 8–12. The crowd-generation and navigation equations remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The substantive central claims remain the ECC task, interactive ECCD benchmark, and zero-shot ATE/NLBN approach balancing counting accuracy against exploration cost. v2 describes ZECC as a baseline and consolidates the contribution bullets, but retains these claims and the best-trade-off assertion. The additional experiments primarily supply supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 identifies a concrete failure condition: building occlusion can cause the MLLM to skip low-altitude exploration over crowds (Appendix E). The conclusion explicitly defers dynamic targets and further real-world application. It also corrects the cluster-size explanation to associate smaller clusters with more navigation points and interprets the new MVC and real-world findings.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's brief implementation paragraph, v2 supplies ATE/NLBN pseudocode, the actual MLLM prompt and panoramic input arrangement, Open3D normal estimation, and 0.25 m voxel deduplication. It also adds CPU/GPU/RAM specifications, real-drone reconstruction and control details, manual annotation information, and a code repository link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including OpenFly, AerialVG, CountFormer, and VGGT, plus a structured dataset comparison in Table 1. It emphasizes ZECC's role as a baseline for the new task. The central positioning between passive crowd counting and embodied navigation remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Substantial introduction, NLBN, and experimental discussion passages are rewritten or condensed. Experimental settings and results become separate top-level sections, while a case-study subsection, acknowledgments, checklist, and organized appendices substantially restructure the document.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. v1 Figures 3–4 become panels of v2 Figure 2; sensitivity plots are regrouped beside a new budget plot. New dataset, MVC, occlusion, and real-world tables accompany trajectory, prompt, failure-case, and dataset visualizations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparison scope and sparse reproducibility information. Multi-view baselines and controlled budget analyses better test the accuracy–cost claim, while occlusion measurements, a failure case, and limited real-world NLBN tests make applicability more assessable. Exact prompts, pseudocode, and deduplication details materially improve reproducibility. Undefined uncertainty bars and the narrow real-world validation remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these gains.
